summary: Explains where RSVP and the related integrated services protocols fit, and gives guidance for deploying resource reservation at the time. It is an informational statement rather than a protocol specification, discussing what the technology can and cannot do.

eli5.summary: It is advice on when reserving a lane on the internet is a good idea and when it is not.

questions: what are the limitations of rsvp
subtitle: Guidance on when and how to deploy RSVP for quality-of-service reservations

tldr.problem: RSVP and Integrated Services offered the first standardized way to reserve bandwidth and quality-of-service guarantees on the Internet, but they introduced new scalability, security, and policy challenges that needed careful consideration before wide deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The document lays out the applicability and limitations of RSVP, identifies three main deployment issues—scalability on high-bandwidth backbones, security and authentication, and policy control for who can reserve resources—and recommends initial deployment in controlled intranet and ISP environments where these issues are more manageable.
tldr.outcome: RSVP saw limited wide-scale deployment due to the issues identified. Simpler approaches like Differentiated Services (DiffServ) later emerged as alternatives, though the protocol remains in use in some networks.

today: RFC 2208 is informational and not obsoleted. RSVP saw limited deployment in the global Internet due to the scalability and complexity issues it identifies. Alternative approaches like Differentiated Services (DiffServ) became more widely adopted for quality-of-service. RSVP remains in use in some carrier networks and managed environments, but never achieved the ubiquitous deployment on the public internet that was initially envisioned.

sections.title: RSVP: A New Service Model for the Internet
sections.content: RSVP (Resource ReSerVation Protocol) is a signaling protocol that allows applications to tell routers along a network path that they need a certain quality of service: guaranteed bandwidth, bounded delay, or low loss. Paired with Integrated Services, it promised to deliver differentiated service qualities on the Internet, breaking from the original IP model of best-effort delivery where all packets were treated equally. Multimedia applications—video conferences, streaming audio, online games—could potentially use RSVP to reserve bandwidth for interactive quality. The protocol was standardized as a Proposed Standard alongside related specifications, making it the first coordinated attempt to add quality-of-service guarantees to IP networks.
sections.eli5: RSVP is like raising your hand on a busy highway to tell drivers 'I'm coming through here and I need clear lanes.' Without RSVP, all traffic mixes together and important stuff gets delayed.

sections.title: Scalability Limitations
sections.content: Every RSVP reservation requires routers to store state information and make scheduling decisions for that flow. On a high-bandwidth backbone (OC-3 and above), supporting thousands or millions of individual reservations becomes computationally expensive and difficult to implement in hardware. Worse, implementing per-flow packet classification and scheduling at high line rates was technically challenging for the hardware of the mid-1990s. The RFC notes that backbone operators would not want to create a separate reservation for each stream; instead, they would need to aggregate many small flows into larger reservations. However, aggregation standards did not exist at the time, and vendors were developing proprietary solutions. The document recommends not deploying RSVP on high-bandwidth backbones initially, and suggests that future aggregation techniques might help.
sections.eli5: If millions of cars each reserve their own lane, the highway becomes impossible to manage. You need a way to group reservations together, but nobody had figured that out yet.

sections.title: Security and Authentication Concerns
sections.content: RSVP is vulnerable to spoofed reservation requests: a malicious host could send fake reservation messages to lock up router resources or obtain unauthorized service. The security documents in the RSVP submission describe hop-by-hop MD5 checksums using an Integrity object to detect modified or spoofed messages between neighboring routers, but this requires a key infrastructure for managing and distributing keys among routers. At the time, no such key infrastructure was deployed. The RFC acknowledges that denial-of-service risks on the routing layer are not unique to RSVP but apply broadly to routing security, and that addressing them requires solving the larger problem of router key management.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to make a reservation and mess things up, like a fake person claiming they need the highway reserved. You need a way for routers to trust each other, which was still being figured out.

sections.title: Policy Control: Who Can Reserve What
sections.content: RSVP itself provides a mechanism for transporting policy information—rules about who can make reservations and what they can reserve—but the RFC does not define specific policies. Vendors said they would implement proprietary policies in their products, meaning a customer deploying RSVP across multiple vendors would face compatibility headaches. The RSVP Working Group was chartered to develop a standardized simple policy object, but at the time of this RFC, policies remained undefined. Before deploying RSVP, operators should carefully evaluate whether vendor policies meet their needs, knowing that they would likely change as standards developed.
sections.eli5: The rules for who gets to reserve bandwidth need to be set, but nobody had standard rules. Each company had their own rules, so putting different companies' equipment together was messy.

sections.title: Recommended Deployment Approach
sections.content: Given the limitations, the RFC recommends that organizations start with RSVP in controlled environments: intranets (networks within a single organization), multimedia applications within a single administrative domain, or limited ISP environments with a small number of flows. Within an intranet, scalability, security, and policy control are more manageable. The RFC quotes RFC 2026's guidance on Proposed Standards: implementors should use them to gain experience and validate the specification, but deploying Proposed Standards into disruption-sensitive environments is risky because the specification may change.
sections.eli5: Try RSVP in your office's internal network first, where you control everything. Don't use it on the global internet until the problems are solved.

sections.title: Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: The RFC identifies three areas of active research and development needed before wide-scale deployment: scalability through aggregation techniques, security through key infrastructure, and policy control through standardized mechanisms. These are not technical defects but rather recognition that the initial specification addresses core RSVP functionality while deferring larger architectural questions. The document encourages the community to document aggregation techniques and gain experience in limited deployments, with updates to the applicability statement expected as work on these issues progresses. It also mentions other topics beyond RSVP itself, such as third-party setup of reservations and differentiated service approaches.
sections.eli5: The smart engineers knew RSVP needed help in three areas and were already working on it. They told people to be patient and learn from trying it in safe places.
